questions.question: What happens if a plugin's required permissions exceed the host's grant?
options: The plugin runs in a degraded mode with reduced functionality
The plugin fails to initialize and the host rejects activation
The host auto-grants the missing permissions after a warning
The plugin silently ignores the missing capabilities
questions.explanation: Correct! The host's checkPermissions() function returns ok: false when any required tool is missing. The plugin fails to initialize and the host shows an error to the user. Optional tools with fallback modes can degrade gracefully, but required permissions are hard gates.

questions.question: When is a plugin update considered "breaking"?
options: When the download size increases by more than 10%
When a required permission is added or a function signature changes
When the README is rewritten with new branding
questions.explanation: Correct! A breaking change is anything that breaks existing consumers. Adding a required permission (e.g. a new mandatory tool) or changing a function's parameter schema forces hosts to update — this demands a MAJOR version bump under SemVer.

questions.question: Why code-sign plugins instead of just hashing?
options: Hashing is too slow for large packages
Signing proves authorship and integrity; hashing only proves integrity
Hashing doesn't work with binary files
questions.explanation: Correct! A hash (e.g. SHA-256) only proves that the bits haven't changed since hashing. A digital signature proves both integrity and authenticity — it cryptographically binds the package to the publisher's identity, which is essential for trust in a distributed plugin ecosystem.
